Name: Suzann Copeland
Badge: Teacher as Researcher | Sustaining Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

Utilizing multiple modes of texts is really important. Intentional planning and chunking is as well, sometimes for the sake of pace, we try to hurry through things. Stop, talk, do, really helped productivity. Slides even for a small intervention group is very useful! I loved working on text sets as well, I hope to build some this summer.

Think back to a moment during the lesson sequence that stands out. It could be a comment from a student, an unexpected challenge or success, a shift in engagement, or a moment when your own thinking changed. Describe what happened and why this moment feels meaningful to you now. What does it reveal:
I just loved how students who typically get lost in classroom discussions were very eager to participate. I counted the back and forth between my students conversations, and I couldn't get a word in when I was a guest participant. Using the visuals and giving slide prompts really had a huge impact.
As you look over the drafts your students produced in this lesson sequence, what early patterns, surprises, or questions are emerging for you? What aspects of your students’ writing are you most curious to explore more deeply with colleagues during our April regroup? What, if any, questions do you h:
I liked the specific details they were able to come up and remember by watching and listening to the video. I want to share this with my staff-- we could really make an impact. I loved the layered pieces to support their text evidence and how it broke it up. It will be easier for teachers to reach the outcomes they would like.
